title: What is Resurrection?
summary: In the cited passages, resurrection means the dead are raised to life. The New Testament presents Jesus' resurrection as central to Christian hope and describes a future resurrection in which life is bodily yet transformed (1 Corinthians 15).
historical_context: The selected texts present resurrection hope in different settings. Daniel 12:1–3 describes sleepers in the dust awakening; Matthew 28 narrates the discovery of Jesus' empty tomb and appearances; Acts 2 proclaims God raised Jesus; and 1 Corinthians 15 argues for the future resurrection of the dead. These passages show the claims made in the texts, not a survey of what all ancient people believed about death.
canonical_context: Daniel 12:1–3 gives a vision of the dead awakening to different outcomes. The New Testament texts focus first on Jesus: John 11 presents him speaking of resurrection and life, Matthew 28 narrates the empty tomb and appearances, and Acts 2 proclaims that God raised him. Paul then argues that Jesus' resurrection is the firstfruits and foundation of the dead being raised (1 Corinthians 15); Revelation 21 pictures a renewed world where death is no more. The passages connect these hopes while serving different literary purposes.
literary_context: The passages use different forms to explain the hope. Matthew 28 tells an empty-tomb and appearance narrative; Acts 2 is a public proclamation about Jesus; 1 Corinthians 15 answers questions about how the dead are raised and what kind of body they have; and 1 Thessalonians 4 offers comfort to a grieving community. Paul contrasts what is perishable with what is imperishable, so 'spiritual body' in his argument describes transformed life rather than simply disembodied survival.
covenantal_significance: Resurrection links Jesus' fate with the future hope offered to his people. In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul calls Christ the firstfruits and argues that his resurrection means death will not have the final word for those who belong to him. First Thessalonians 4 uses the same hope to comfort grieving readers, while Revelation 21 places it within the vision of a renewed creation without death. Each passage emphasizes a different part of that hope.
canonical_role: What is Resurrection? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: Matthew 28 narrates an empty tomb and appearances, and 1 Corinthians 15 argues for resurrection as transformed bodily life. These texts describe more than a symbol of hope, though historical questions require evidence beyond a summary of the passages.

The New Testament connects Jesus' resurrection with the future resurrection of the dead: Paul calls Christ the firstfruits in 1 Corinthians 15, and 1 Thessalonians 4 uses that hope to comfort readers.
